result.graft: From A, keep the Connect sheet's one-line footer naming Model A as advance notice, so B's first-send sheet confirms rather than surprises.
result.defense: B is the only option with an explicit, named consent moment at the relevant time — first send — plus a drawn declined state that preserves the draft and offers one-tap Allow in context. A technically covers the states but buries recovery in a 4-tap Settings detour from a Not sent row, leaving a first-run founder stuck away from their draft. C recovers in place, but repeats a permission card across Thread, Home and Inbox where Home/Inbox have no send intent, creating nagging clutter, competing prominent actions, and the highest build/state-sync cost. B's sheet-plus-strip stays solid, minimal, and focused with Allow as the sole tinted action.

result.graft: From A, include the Settings off-state line so founders have a permanent, discoverable place to manage the toggle after turning it on in place.
result.defense: C wins because it preserves the streamlined Connect sheet footer while solving the declined and allow-later gaps proactively and in context. With Send disabled and the draft preserved, the permission placeholder card's 'Turn on' button cleanly serves as the view's single tinted prominent action alongside a minimal disclosure line, enabling one-tap recovery. In contrast, A forces the user into a reactive 'Not sent' failure state and a high-friction 4-tap detour through Settings to resume work. B regresses product architecture by reintroducing the previously removed modal consent sheet on first send and adds an 'Allow' strip that competes with the composer's primary action.
